title: Triples with Bitwise AND Equal To Zero
statement: You get an integer array `nums`. Count the ordered index triples `(i, j, k)`, where each of `i`, `j` and `k` may be any index from `0` to `nums.length - 1` (the same index may be used more than once), for which `nums[i] & nums[j] & nums[k]` is `0`, with `&` meaning bitwise AND. Return that count.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every triple is O(n³), about 10⁹ steps for 1000 numbers. The values have only 16 bits, though, so `nums[i] & nums[j]` has at most 2^16 possible results. Count how many index pairs produce each result once, in O(n²). Then a triple works exactly when the pair's AND shares no bit with the third number, so for each third number only the pair results that fit inside its complement matter.

## Approach

1. OR all numbers into `full`. Every AND of the numbers uses only bits of `full`, so a table of `full + 1` slots is enough (at most 2^16).
2. Fill `pairs`, where `pairs[v]` is the number of ordered pairs `(i, j)` with `nums[i] & nums[j] === v`.
3. For each `third` number, take `free = full & ~third`, the bits of `full` that `third` lacks. A pair result works when all of its bits lie inside `free`, that is, when it is a submask of `free`.
4. Walk through every submask of `free` with `mask = (mask - 1) & free`, starting at `free` and finishing at `0`, and add `pairs[mask]` to `count`.
5. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 1, 3]`, so `full = 3` and `pairs` has 4 slots. The nine ordered pairs give `pairs[0] = 2` (2&1, 1&2), `pairs[1] = 3`, `pairs[2] = 3` and `pairs[3] = 1`.

- `third = 2`: `free = 1`, whose submasks are 1 and 0: `3 + 2 = 5`.
- `third = 1`: `free = 2`, submasks 2 and 0: `3 + 2 = 5`.
- `third = 3`: `free = 0`, only 0: `2`.

The total is `5 + 5 + 2 = 12`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² + n·2^16) in the worst case: the pair table takes n² steps, and a `free` with f bits has 2^f submasks to visit.
- Space: O(2^16) for `pairs`, less when the values use fewer bits.

## Pitfalls

- Indices may repeat and order matters, so loop over all n² pairs, not only `i < j`.
- `~third` alone is negative in JavaScript; masking it with `full` keeps only meaningful bits and a valid table index.
- The submask loop must still visit `0`, so add `pairs[mask]` before checking whether `mask` is `0`.
- The answer can reach 10⁹ = 1000³, which still fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `full` | OR of all values: every bit any value uses |
| `pairs` | `pairs[v]`: ordered pairs whose AND equals `v` |
| `first`, `second` | the two values of a pair |
| `third` | the value that completes the triple |
| `free` | the bits of `full` that `third` does not have |
| `mask` | the current submask of `free` |
| `count` | triples found so far |

narration.2: Start the OR of all values at zero.
narration.3: Collect every bit that any value uses; no AND of the values can have a bit outside full.
narration.4: One counter per possible pair result, from 0 up to full.
narration.5: Pick the first value of an ordered pair...
narration.6: ...and the second; the same index may be used twice.
narration.7: Count this pair under its AND result.
narration.12: Now try every value as the third member of the triple.
narration.13: The bits third lacks; a pair result works only if all of its bits are among these.
narration.14: Visit every submask of free, from free itself down to 0.
narration.15: Every pair whose AND equals this submask completes a zero triple with third.
narration.16: Zero is the last submask, so stop after counting it.
narration.19: Return the number of ordered triples whose AND is zero.
